Comment: Holds spatial maps of initial visual features and integrates visual information across the entire visual field in the first stage of visual search. Receives retinotopically organized projections from V1-V3 and represents the position and basic features (orientation, spatial frequency) of visual stimuli. Executes comparison of low-level features during visual search. Includes IPS1-2.
Output Semantics: [U.pIPS] Spatial priority map of visual features across the entire visual field. Encodes behavioral priority at each spatial location by integrating visual salience (bottom-up saliency) and task relevance (top-down relevance). Maintains basic features of visual stimuli (position, orientation, color, shape, motion) in retinotopic coordinates and codes initial match with search goals as a spatial map.
Requirement: [U.pIPS] must construct a spatial priority map of visual stimuli across an extended visual field to realize perceptual speed. Input: [U.V1] ([V1] Retinotopic visual feature maps of orientation, spatial frequency, color, luminance contrast); [U.V2] ([V2] More complex visual features such as contours, textures, stereoscopic disparity); [U.V3] ([V3] Representations of global motion patterns and dynamic forms); [U.V4] ([V4] Integrated representations of color constancy and form, combination features of object color and shape); [U.MT] ([MT] Selective representations of visual motion direction and speed, optical flow patterns); [U.IT] ([IT] High-level representations of object categories and forms, identity representations of visual stimuli such as letters, numbers, and complex patterns); [U.Pulvinar] ([Pulvinar] Fast visual information relay via superior colliculus, attention modulation signals, subcortical pathway for visual salience); [U.FEF] ([FEF] Attention control signals specifying spatial locations and features to search); [U.DLPFC] ([DLPFC] Search goal templates, task rules). By integrating these inputs, [U.pIPS] computes behavioral priority combining visual salience (bottom-up saliency) and task relevance (top-down relevance) at each spatial location and outputs a spatial priority map to [U.mIPS], [U.V1], [U.V2], [U.V3], [U.V4], [U.MT], and [U.FEF]. This transformation determines which regions of the visual field should be processed preferentially as the first stage of visual search, enhancing the efficiency of perceptual speed.
Requirement realization by interface: The Interface of [U.pIPS], defined as ([U.mIPS], [U.V1], [U.V2], [U.V3], [U.V4], [U.MT], [U.FEF]) = [U.pIPS]([U.V1], [U.V2], [U.V3], [U.V4], [U.MT], [U.IT], [U.Pulvinar], [U.FEF], [U.DLPFC]), realizes the function described in the Requirement as follows: Bottom-up visual feature information from early visual areas ([U.V1], [U.V2], [U.V3], [U.V4], [U.MT]), object identity information from [U.IT], and subcortical fast visual information from [U.Pulvinar] are integrated as inputs. Simultaneously, top-down attention control signals from [U.FEF] and search goal templates from [U.DLPFC] are input to modulate task relevance. The integrated spatial priority map is sent to [U.mIPS], and furthermore, feedback projections to visual areas ([U.V1]-[U.MT]) realize attentional sensitivity modulation, while feedback to [U.FEF] conveys candidate locations for attention shifts. This Interface fully supports the bottom-up and top-down integration required in the Requirement and the transmission of priority information to downstream UCs.
Capability: Capability to construct a spatial map representing behavioral priority by integrating bottom-up stimulus-driven information and top-down goal-driven information. This capability includes computation that transforms multiple different information sources (initial visual features, object representations, attention control signals, search goals) into a common spatial coordinate system and assigns a single priority value to each spatial location. Priority map computation is realized through automatic extraction of visual saliency and multiplicative or additive integration with task-goal weighting. This mechanism is theorized in Itti & Koch's (2001) Saliency map model, Bisley & Goldberg's (2010) Priority map theory, and Wolfe's (2021) Guided Search 6.0 model. Neuroscientifically, LIP neurons have been demonstrated at the single-neuron level to additively integrate visual signals, saccadic signals, and cognitive signals (Thomas & Paré, 2007). Priority maps are feature-independent and function universally for various visual stimuli (letters, numbers, patterns).
Mechanism: Priority map construction is realized through the following computational steps. First, local salience is computed in each visual feature channel (orientation, color, motion, etc.). This is implemented as local contrast detection by center-surround difference filters. Salience maps from each feature channel are normalized and integrated across feature dimensions (Winner-take-all or weighted sum). This forms the bottom-up saliency map. In parallel, top-down signals (from [U.FEF] and [U.DLPFC]) enhance weights of spatial locations with features matching the search goal. This is implemented as similarity computation between goal templates and visual features (e.g., template matching, distance computation in feature space). Bottom-up saliency map and top-down relevance map are multiplicatively or additively integrated to form the final priority map. Activity at each location in the priority map is proportional to the probability of attention allocation and saccade execution to that location. Surround suppression mechanisms sharpen the priority map spatially, emphasizing the location with highest priority. The priority map is dynamically updated, and priority of already visited locations decreases as search progresses (inhibition of return).
Implementation: Bottom-up saliency: S_bu(x,y) = Σ_i w_i * N(F_i(x,y)) where F_i(x,y): salience at location (x,y) in feature channel i, N(): normalization function, w_i: channel weight; Top-down relevance: S_td(x,y) = sim(V(x,y), T) where V(x,y): visual feature vector at location (x,y) (from [U.V1]-[U.MT]), T: search goal template (from [U.DLPFC]), sim(): similarity function; Priority map: P(x,y) = α * S_bu(x,y) + β * S_td(x,y) + γ * A(x,y) where A(x,y): attention control signal from [U.FEF], α, β, γ: integration weights; Surround suppression: P'(x,y) = P(x,y) - k * ∫∫ G(x-x', y-y') * P(x',y') dx'dy' where G(): Gaussian kernel, k: suppression strength; [U.pIPS] = P'(x,y)

Comment: Responsible for integration of visual features and allocation of attention. Receives information from posterior IPS and integrates feature-based and spatial-based attention. Compares the search goal (template) with current visual information, selecting target candidates. Includes IPS3.
Output Semantics: [U.mIPS] Representations of visual target candidates selected by attention. Weighted representations of multiple target candidates in visual search and suppression signals for distractors. Adaptive attention allocation patterns according to target set size and distractor set size. Priority weighting signals for allowing behaviorally relevant items to access short-term memory. Dynamic allocation state of visuospatial attention.
Requirement: [U.mIPS] must select target candidates from among multiple visual stimuli in the visual field and suppress distractors to realize perceptual speed. Input: [U.pIPS] ([pIPS] Spatial priority map of visual features across the entire visual field); [U.FEF] ([FEF] Attention allocation control signals, adjustment of search strategy); [U.DLPFC] ([DLPFC] Working memory contents and executive control, information maintenance during search). Based on the priority map from [U.pIPS], [U.mIPS] adaptively allocates attentional resources to multiple target candidates while suppressing interference from distractors. It dynamically adjusts attention allocation patterns according to target set size and distractor set size. Selected candidates and their weighting information are output to [U.aIPS] and [U.FEF]. This transformation realizes narrowing down of candidates and concentration of attention as an intermediate stage in visual search, enhancing "comparison efficiency" in perceptual speed.
Requirement realization by interface: The Interface of [U.mIPS], defined as ([U.aIPS], [U.FEF]) = [U.mIPS]([U.pIPS], [U.FEF], [U.DLPFC]), realizes the function described in the Requirement as follows: The spatial priority map from [U.pIPS] is input, providing initial information about which spatial locations are behaviorally important. Attention allocation control signals from [U.FEF] and working memory contents from [U.DLPFC] (detailed search goals, task rules) are input to modulate target candidate selection criteria. [U.mIPS] integrates these inputs to select target candidates and sends this information to [U.aIPS] to prepare for detection judgment. Simultaneously, by feeding back selection results and attention requirements to [U.FEF], it forms an attention shift control loop. This Interface fully supports priority map-based candidate selection, top-down modulation, and transmission of selection information downstream as required in the Requirement.
Capability: Capability of selective attention to select behaviorally relevant items (target candidates) from among multiple visual stimuli and suppress behaviorally irrelevant items (distractors). This capability includes computation that controls access rights to visual short-term memory and adaptively allocates attentional resources according to target set size and distractor set size. In the Guided Search 6.0 model (Wolfe, 2021), items are sequentially processed from high-activity locations in the priority map, with each item undergoing a diffusion-based recognition process (>150ms/item). In the VS-SAIM model (Heinke & Humphreys, 2003), parallel competitive processes in the selection and object identification stages realize attention selection. Neuroscientifically, mIPS codes visuospatial attention (Ptak & Schnider, 2011) and shows asymptotic activity increase for target set size, with suppressive effects appearing when distractors are present (Gillebert et al., 2012). Feature attention functions as a mechanism controlling the balance between search speed and accuracy (Vater et al., 2023).
Mechanism: Selective attention is realized through the following computational mechanisms. From the priority map from [U.pIPS], attention spotlights are sequentially placed at locations where activity reaches peaks. Within each attention spotlight, visual features are compared with the goal template from [U.DLPFC] (template matching). Items whose match exceeds a threshold are selected as target candidates and their weights are enhanced. For distractors, a "pop-in" mechanism as observed in V4 (sustained suppression after initial enhancement) is applied. When multiple targets exist, attentional resources are divided and allocated to each candidate. When distractor set size is large, suppression processes are strengthened. Knowledge-based on-centre-off-surround receptive field mechanisms automatically suppress distractors surrounding selected items (VS-SAIM model). Feature attention strength is dynamically adjusted to minimize search time cost and error cost. The selection process is implemented as parallel competition, with mutual inhibition working among multiple candidates and the strongest candidate becoming the winner (Winner-take-all mechanism).
Implementation: Attention spotlight placement: A(x,y,t) = Θ(P(x,y,t) - θ_att) where P(x,y,t): priority map from [U.pIPS] at time t, Θ: step function, θ_att: attention threshold; Template matching: M_i = sim(V_i, T) where V_i: visual features at location i, T: goal template from [U.DLPFC], sim(): similarity; Target selection: S_i = M_i * A_i - Σ_{j≠i} w_ij * S_j where w_ij: competitive mutual inhibition weight; Distractor suppression: D_i(t) = max(0, I_i(t) - k * (I_i(t-Δt) + Σ_j w_ij * S_j)) where I_i: initial activity of item i, k: suppression coefficient; Feature attention modulation: F = arg min (C_time * RT + C_error * ER) where F: feature attention strength, RT: reaction time, ER: error rate, C_time, C_error: cost weights; [U.mIPS] = {S_i | S_i > θ_sel}, θ_sel: selection threshold

Comment: Integrates search results and bridges to decision-making. Computes confidence in target detection and is involved in search termination judgment. Has strong connections with frontal cortex and transforms detection results into motor responses and decision-making. Includes IPS4.
Output Semantics: [U.aIPS] Decision confidence regarding target detection. Neural population code representing subjective certainty of visual discrimination judgment. Simultaneously represents binary judgment of whether target exists or not and reliability of that judgment. Motor execution preparation signals (saccades, manual responses). Accumulated state of evidence needed for search termination judgment. Confidence emerges approximately 300ms after stimulus presentation and persists until motor response.
Requirement: [U.aIPS] must judge whether a target has been detected and compute confidence in that judgment as the final stage of visual search to realize perceptual speed. Input: [U.mIPS] ([mIPS] Representations of visual target candidates selected by attention, weighted representations, suppression signals for distractors); [U.FEF] ([FEF] Control signals for search termination and response initiation); [U.DLPFC] ([DLPFC] Decision criteria and response rules, threshold control for detection judgment). Evidence of target candidates sent from [U.mIPS] is temporally accumulated and compared with judgment criteria (from [U.DLPFC]) to determine presence or absence of target detection. Simultaneously, based on accumulated evidence strength and accumulation time, confidence in that judgment is computed. Confidence emerges approximately 300ms after stimulus presentation and persists until motor response. Detection judgment and confidence are output to [U.pIPS], [U.mIPS] (feedback for continuing search judgment), [U.FEF], [U.DLPFC] (providing evidence for decision-making), [U.SC], [U.PMC] (motor response execution). This transformation optimizes the speed-accuracy tradeoff in "judgment speed and accuracy" in perceptual speed.
Requirement realization by interface: The Interface of [U.aIPS], defined as ([U.pIPS], [U.mIPS], [U.FEF], [U.DLPFC], [U.SC], [U.PMC]) = [U.aIPS]([U.mIPS], [U.FEF], [U.DLPFC]), realizes the function described in the Requirement as follows: Target candidate information from [U.mIPS] is input, providing evidence for detection judgment. Search termination control signals from [U.FEF] and decision criteria (detection threshold) from [U.DLPFC] are input to modulate judgment timing and criteria. [U.aIPS] accumulates evidence, computes judgment and confidence, and sends results to [U.FEF] and [U.DLPFC] to close the cognitive control loop. Simultaneously, outputs to [U.SC] and [U.PMC] initiate motor responses. Furthermore, feedback to [U.pIPS] and [U.mIPS] controls whether search should continue or terminate. This Interface supports all aspects required in the Requirement: evidence accumulation, judgment/confidence computation, cognitive control feedback, and motor output.
Capability: Capability to temporally accumulate sensory evidence and simultaneously compute binary judgment (target present/absent) and confidence in that judgment. This capability includes computation that derives statistically optimal judgments from noisy sensory inputs and metacognitively evaluates judgment reliability. The Drift Diffusion Model (DDM) provides a standard description of evidence accumulation processes, where judgment is made when evidence reaches a threshold (Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008). Confidence computation explicitly includes not only final evidence level but also decision time and post-decisional accumulation (Navajas et al., 2024). Bayesian confidence models (POMDP; Sanders et al., 2016) provide a normative approach defining confidence as "posterior probability that judgment is correct." Neuroscientifically, parietal cortex neurons represent confidence associated with decisions as population codes (Kiani & Shadlen, 2009). Confidence signals emerge approximately 300ms after stimulus presentation and persist until motor response (Gherman & Philiastides, 2015).
Mechanism: Judgment and confidence computation are realized through the following mechanisms. Evidence of target candidates sent from [U.mIPS] (selection strength) is temporally integrated as a noisy diffusion process. Evidence accumulation occurs in parallel in two independent integrators (accumulators) representing target hypothesis and no-target hypothesis. At each time step, increments proportional to sensory evidence drift rate and Gaussian noise are added to integrators. When either integrator reaches decision threshold (set by [U.DLPFC]), judgment is finalized. Confidence is computed as a function of "evidence amount in winner integrator" minus "evidence amount in loser integrator" at judgment time, and time taken for judgment. Specifically, Confidence ∝ (Evidence_winner - Evidence_loser) / Decision_time. Alternatively, in Bayesian models, Confidence = P(correct | evidence, choice, time). Evidence accumulation continues after judgment (post-decisional accumulation), contributing to confidence updating. Confidence emerges as neural activity approximately 300ms after stimulus presentation and is maintained in parallel with motor preparation signals. When threshold is high, judgment is slow but confidence is high; when threshold is low, judgment is fast but confidence is low (speed-accuracy tradeoff).
Implementation: Evidence accumulation (Drift Diffusion Model): dE_target/dt = μ_target * S + σ * η(t), dE_notarget/dt = μ_notarget * (1-S) + σ * η(t) where E: accumulated evidence, μ: drift rate, S: sensory evidence from [U.mIPS], σ: noise strength, η(t): Gaussian noise; Decision: Choice = arg max(E_target, E_notarget) if max(E_target, E_notarget) > θ_decision where θ_decision: decision threshold from [U.DLPFC]; Decision time: RT = t when max(E_target, E_notarget) = θ_decision; Confidence (evidence-based): Conf = (max(E_target, E_notarget) - min(E_target, E_notarget)) / RT; Confidence (Bayesian): Conf = P(correct | E, Choice, RT) = ∫ P(correct | drift_rate) * P(drift_rate | E, Choice, RT) d(drift_rate); Post-decisional accumulation: E(t) = E(RT) + ∫_{RT}^{t} (μ * S(τ) + σ * η(τ)) dτ for t > RT; [U.aIPS] = (Choice, Conf)
